beats.intro: Module four. [[sub]]How companies and banks borrow short term, and how the repo market works.
beats.lines: Companies often borrow short term from banks. [[unc]]An uncommitted line of credit is the most flexible and cheapest. There is no fee, except interest on what is used. But the bank can refuse to lend, so it is the least reliable. [[reg]]A committed line is a formal written promise, usually for up to three hundred sixty four days, often shared by a syndicate of banks. It costs a commitment fee, for example half a percent. [[rev]]A revolving credit agreement is a multiyear commitment, and the most reliable. Lenders add covenants, as in a bond indenture.
beats.secured: Weaker borrowers pledge collateral. [[sec]]A secured loan, or asset-based loan, is backed by assets such as equipment, receivables, or inventory, and the lender files a lien. [[assign]]With an assignment of receivables, the company uses them as collateral, and still collects the payments. [[factor]]With factoring, it sells the receivables at a discount to a factor, which takes over the collection.
beats.cp: Strong companies can skip the bank and issue commercial paper. [[a]]These are short-term, unsecured notes, usually under three months, from large, highly rated issuers. They fund working capital, seasonal needs, or bridge financing. [[roll]]Maturing paper is usually paid with new paper. That creates rollover risk. [[back]]So investors require a committed backup line from banks, to repay if a rollover fails. [[who]]Financial institutions issue about sixty percent of the volume, and governments and supranationals issue too. Paper sold internationally is called Eurocommercial paper.
beats.banks: Banks have their own short-term funding. [[dep]]Deposits are the main source. Demand deposits can be withdrawn at any time, but are a stable source in normal times. [[cd]]Certificates of deposit have a fixed term and rate, and negotiable ones can be sold before maturity. [[ib]]In the interbank market, banks lend to each other, from overnight to a year. [[cb]]Banks short of required reserves borrow in the central bank funds market, at the central bank funds rate. As a last resort, they borrow from the central bank itself, at a higher rate, with collateral. [[cpp]]Banks also issue commercial paper, and a secured form called asset-backed commercial paper.
beats.abcp: Asset-backed commercial paper works in two steps. [[s1]]First, a bank transfers short-term loans to a special purpose entity, in exchange for cash. [[s2]]Second, the entity issues commercial paper to investors, backed by the loans, with a backup liquidity line from the bank. [[off]]The financing stays off the bank's balance sheet. [[crisis]]Before the financial crisis, many entities funded long-term assets this way. When they could not roll the paper, many failed. Today it mostly funds short-term, high-quality loans.
beats.repo: A repurchase agreement, or repo, is a secured short-term loan. [[sell]]One side sells a security today, for cash, and agrees to buy it back later at a higher price. [[ex]]Say a Treasury note worth one hundred million dollars. [[leg1]]The buyer pays one hundred million, and takes the note. [[leg2]]Thirty days later, the seller pays back one hundred million plus interest, at a repo rate of point two five percent, and gets the note back. [[calc]]Interest is one hundred million, times point two five percent, times thirty over three hundred sixty. That is twenty thousand, eight hundred thirty three dollars. [[roles]]The security seller is the cash borrower. The security buyer is the cash lender, and is said to do a reverse repo.
beats.margin: To protect the lender, repos use excess collateral. [[im]]An initial margin of one hundred two percent means the collateral is worth two percent more than the cash lent. [[loan]]So for a one hundred million dollar note, the loan is about ninety eight point zero four million. The haircut is one point nine six percent. [[var]]If the note rises in value, say to one hundred three million, the loan is over-collateralized. [[rel]]The borrower can ask for about two point nine one million of notes to be released. If the price falls, the lender can ask for more collateral. This adjustment is called variation margin.
beats.uses: The repo market has three main uses. [[inc]]Lenders earn short-term income on a secured basis, with minimal liquidity or default risk. [[fin]]Dealers finance their inventory of securities, borrowing most of the purchase price against the bonds. [[cbk]]And central banks use repos to add or drain cash in the banking system, for short-term policy. [[short]]Repos also help investors sell short, as the next steps show.
beats.short: Here is a short sale through a repo, in four steps. [[s1]]The hedge fund lends one hundred million in cash, and receives the Treasury note. [[s2]]It sells the note in the market, for one hundred million. [[s3]]Thirty days later, it buys the note back for ninety nine million. [[s4]]It delivers the note, and receives the repurchase price of one hundred million, twenty thousand, eight hundred thirty three dollars. [[pl]]The profit is one million, twenty thousand, eight hundred thirty three dollars, before costs. It profits because the price fell.
beats.rates: Repo rates depend on four things. [[mm]]Money market rates, which central banks influence. [[col]]Collateral quality. Riskier collateral means a higher rate. [[term]]The term. Longer repos usually cost more. [[uniq]]And how special the collateral is. When many investors want one particular bond, its repo rate falls, even below zero.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]Short-term bank funding ranges from uncommitted lines to revolvers. [[w2]]Commercial paper is cheap, but needs a backup line for rollover risk. [[w3]]A repo is a collateralized loan: sell now, buy back later. [[w4]]Margin protects lenders, and repo rates depend on collateral and demand.
